title: Toxic Workplace Dynamics
situation: Grace, a 32-year-old, is dealing with a passive-aggressive manager who undermines her in meetings and takes credit for her work. She is unsure whether to escalate or leave.
user_turns: My manager constantly undermines me in meetings and takes credit for my ideas. I've tried addressing it directly but nothing changes. I don't know whether to escalate to HR or just leave.
I've documented some incidents but I'm scared that if I go to HR it will make things worse and I'll be seen as a troublemaker.
I've been at this company for four years and I don't want to throw that away. But I also can't keep working in this environment. How do I decide what to do?
What does assertive communication actually look like in this situation? I don't want to come across as aggressive.

title: Divorce and Co-Parenting Conflict
situation: Michael, a 40-year-old, is going through a difficult divorce. He and his ex-wife disagree on parenting decisions and the conflict is affecting their children.
user_turns: My divorce is getting messy. My ex and I can't agree on anything about the kids and every conversation turns into an argument. I'm worried about how this is affecting them.
She undermines my parenting decisions in front of the children. I try to stay calm but I end up getting defensive and it escalates.
My kids are 8 and 11. They've started acting out at school. I know it's because of the tension between us but I don't know how to fix it.
How do I communicate with someone who refuses to cooperate? I can't force her to change but I can't keep going like this.

title: Career Crossroads
situation: Helen, a 35-year-old, has a stable but unfulfilling career in finance. She wants to change careers to something more meaningful but is afraid of the financial and social consequences.
user_turns: I've been in finance for ten years and I'm good at it but I hate it. I want to do something more meaningful — maybe social work or counseling — but I'm scared to give up the salary and status.
My family thinks I'm crazy for even considering it. They sacrificed a lot for me to get this career. I feel guilty for wanting something different.
I'm 35. Is it too late to start over? I'd have to go back to school and take a massive pay cut. I don't know if I can justify that.
How do I figure out if this is a genuine calling or just burnout? I don't want to make a huge life change and regret it.

title: Boundary Setting with Family
situation: Amy, a 28-year-old, has an overbearing mother who calls multiple times a day, gives unsolicited advice, and makes Amy feel guilty for having her own life. Amy wants to set boundaries but fears damaging the relationship.
user_turns: My mother calls me three or four times a day and gets upset if I don't answer. She gives me unsolicited advice about everything and makes me feel guilty for having my own life.
I love her but I feel suffocated. Every time I try to create some distance she cries and says I don't care about her. Then I feel terrible and give in.
I've tried to talk to her about it but she doesn't see anything wrong with her behaviour. She thinks she's just being a caring mother.
How do I set limits with someone who doesn't respect them? I don't want to hurt her but I need space.

title: Recovering from Infidelity
situation: Tom, a 38-year-old, discovered his wife had an affair six months ago. They are trying to rebuild the relationship but he is struggling with trust, anger, and self-doubt.
user_turns: I found out my wife had an affair six months ago. We're trying to work through it but I can't stop thinking about it. I check her phone, I question everything she says. I hate who I've become.
She says she's sorry and it's over. I want to believe her but I can't. Every time she's late or doesn't answer her phone I spiral.
I don't know if I can ever trust her again. But I also don't want to end the marriage. We have kids. We have a life together. Is it even possible to rebuild trust after this?
What does rebuilding trust actually look like in practice? I don't know what I'm supposed to be doing.

title: Addiction Recovery Support
situation: Chris, a 33-year-old, has been sober from alcohol for three months after years of heavy drinking. He is struggling with cravings, social pressure, and rebuilding his self-image.
user_turns: I've been sober for three months. It's the longest I've gone in years. But the cravings are still really strong, especially in social situations.
My friends still drink and they don't really understand why I stopped. They keep offering me drinks and saying 'just one won't hurt.' It's exhausting.
I'm also struggling with who I am without alcohol. I used it to socialise, to relax, to cope with stress. I don't know how to do those things sober.
How do I handle social situations where everyone is drinking without feeling like an outsider or having to explain myself every time?
